headlines.summary: CoreWeave shares are down 35% in October, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave's stock is down 35% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening. The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds. In this article CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 35% this month after plunging 8% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. CoreWeave's stock move this month The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 171% in the past year and 36% in October. It last stood at 1,115 basis points, or 11.15%. CoreWeave declined to comment. The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 32% this month, while IREN's stock is down 39%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. On hold until midterms CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft . That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing. Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. watch now VIDEO 2:39 02:39 CoreWeave falls amid AI debt fears Power Lunch CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options. "Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant." CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter." Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary? Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors. "Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute." — CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report. headlines.title: Musk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. Few exist
headlines.summary: Governments or companies looking for an alternative to SpaceX's Starlink are faced with few options, as Amazon, Eutelsat and others are far behind.
headlines.article_text: Elon Musk's Ukraine clash accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Ukraine's problems with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield have accelerated demand for alternative satellite internet services. Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after reports that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered speed limits on Starshield service in the country. Amazon, Eutelsat and sovereign operators have raced to build out constellations, but they have yet to catch up with SpaceX. In this article SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Soldiers from a separate task rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in the Zaporizhzhia region set up a Starlink satellite communication terminal at a combat position in the Donetsk region, Ukraine, Oct. 16, 2026. Dmytro Smolienko | Ukrinform | Future Publishing | Getty Images Elon Musk 's latest clash with Ukraine underscores the critical role that his company's Starlink satellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022. It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering. On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself. SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits on Starshield . SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology." The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 miles per hour that Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander told The New York Times the Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by 3 days. Musk and President Donald Trump, both critics of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation. On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place. Trump insisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved." Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger " that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication." "People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power." watch now VIDEO 1:05 01:05 Pres. Trump: Don't know who ordered Starlink slowdown in Ukraine, but 'I was not involved' Closing Bell: Overtime The disruptions have prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful." "There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a "Squawk on the Street" interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake." Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in a social media post Wednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine." On SpaceX's earnings call this week, executives didn't address the issue and weren't asked about it by analysts. Starlink dominance Governments or companies looking for an alternative to Musk, SpaceX and its satellite internet services have few options. Amazon 's Leo , which also delivers internet connectivity via a low Earth orbit satellite constellation, is seven years in the making and has yet to fully come online, with only 390 satellites in orbit. SpaceX, by comparison, boasts a Starlink constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan C. McDowell . Starlink connectivity is live in 174 countries, SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on Tuesday's earnings call. Blue Origin , Jeff Bezos' space company, in January unveiled a service called TeraWave for enterprise and government customers. It's targeting deployment of the first batch of satellites in the fourth quarter of 2027. France's Eutelsat, also a competitor to Starlink, has more than 600 satellites in orbit. The stock surged 23% on Oct. 14 as reports emerged that Musk had restricted Starlink in Ukraine. Several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems. The EU is building IRIS² , which is expected to span hundreds of satellites, but the first launches aren't expected until 2029. Most of these planned systems are unlikely to "come anywhere close" in terms of capacity, coverage, resilience or cost compared to Starlink, said Christian Freiherr von der Ropp, an independent satellite consultant. The cost, size, weight and power draw of Eutelsat's terminals make them particularly unsuitable in the battlefield, he added. While SpaceX's Connectivity business has raced ahead of rivals, the company also has the advantage of overseeing a hugely successful rocket launch business, which has carried satellites to orbit for many of its competitors. SpaceX is now phasing out commercial rides on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket, while it tests and develops its massive Starship rocket. Many new constellations "could therefore face substantial delays and materially higher launch costs," von der Ropp said. A Ukrainian uses a Starlink satellite-internet communication system on a rooftop in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Tuesday, March 11, 2025. Andrew Kravchenko | Bloomberg | Getty Images This week, Ukraine and European lawmakers moved to explore alternatives to Starlink, framing the issue as a matter of national security. Their concern is that access to a critical communications service could potentially be disrupted "as a consequence of Musk's political agenda," said von der Ropp. "The degree of soft power SpaceX has accumulated over companies, governments and militaries is substantial, and that has now become very visible," von der Ropp said. "Inevitably, this is creating mistrust and accelerating demand for alternatives." Zelenskyy wrote Wednesday in a post on X that he met with Norwegian officials and Kongsberg, a Norwegian defense company, to discuss air defense systems and "launching work on new satellite communication capabilities for our warriors." Musk enjoyed accolades for providing Starlink terminals and satellite internet service during the early days of the war, but relations have soured between the world's richest person and Ukrainian officials over the years. Musk previously ordered SpaceX engineers to shut off Starlink's satellite network over Crimea to thwart a Ukrainian attack on Russian warships, according to a chapter in the 2023 Musk biography written by Walter Isaacson. Musk disputed the report. The revelation drew rebuke from Ukrainian officials, including a top Zelenskyy aide, who said it led to Ukrainian civilians being killed. headlines.article_text: Comcast (CMCSA) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Comcast topped analyst earnings expectations for the third quarter. Streaming service Peacock hit profitability for the second consecutive quarter. Comcast is in the process of spinning off its media business into a separate publicly traded company. Theme parks and the connectivity business continued to face pressure. In this article CMCSA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:54 02:54 Comcast beats on top and bottom lines in Q3 Squawk Box Comcast beat Wall Street's expectations for third-quarter earnings — despite headwinds in its theme parks business — thanks to continued strength in its media unit. The company's Peacock streaming service reported a quarterly profit for the second time since its launch in 2020, posting $261 million in adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization on $1.8 billion in revenue. Peacock maintained 48 million paid subscribers, flat from last quarter and up 17% year over year. Comcast said the streamer demonstrated strong retention despite raising subscription prices in August. The platform continued to reap the benefits of record-high viewership for the FIFA World Cup, as the final games played out at the beginning of the quarter and aired on NBCUniversal's Telemundo and on Peacock. Revenue in Comcast's media division, which includes the streaming service, rose 13% compared with the third quarter last year to $5.4 billion. The overall content and experiences unit, which also includes its film studio and theme parks, saw revenue rise 6.5%. Comcast's connectivity and platforms sector, however, continued to face pressure, with revenue down 2.7% year over year. The company reported a net loss in domestic broadband residential customers of 144,000 and a net loss in its cable customers of 274,000 during the period. Its mobile business added 368,000 customers. After years of stagnating growth in broadband and heightened competition from wireless providers like Verizon and T-Mobile, Comcast announced in January 2025 that it would refocus on its mobile business and pursue more competitive pricing plans. "We feel mobile remains a tremendous growth opportunity for us. It's a capital light model, [which] leverages our existing customer broadband base," Steve Croney, CEO of Comcast's connectivity and platforms division, said on an earnings call on Thursday. Shares of Comcast rose roughly 5% following the report. Here's how Comcast performed for the period ended Sept. 30 compared with what analysts expected, according to LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.07 adjusted vs. 98 cents expected Revenue: $29.3 billion vs. $29.28 billion expected In June, Comcast announced plans to spin off NBCUniversal and European media business Sky from its core cable, wireless and business services units. The split, which Comcast said would take about a year, will create two separate publicly traded companies. Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said on the earnings call that the company is "on track" to complete the transaction by mid-2027. "While there is still significant work ahead, we have a clear path to completion and remain focused on creating two companies with the strategic flexibility, financial strength, and leadership to compete and grow independently," Cavanagh said. "We have tremendous confidence in the future of both companies." The split comes after Comcast spun off most of its cable networks , along with an array of digital businesses, into Versant . That separation was completed in January. For the third quarter, Comcast's revenue was 6% lower than the year-ago period. However, adjusting for the impact of the Versant spin, revenue was essentially flat year over year, Comcast said. Net income for the period was $3.45 billion, or 97 cents per share, compared with $3.33 billion, or 90 cents per share, in the third quarter of 2025. Adjusting for one-time items, including investments and the value of certain intangible assets, Comcast reported adjusted earnings per share of $1.07. The company's theme park revenue fell 4.4% during the period to $2.6 billion, which the company attributed to "cyclical headwinds" and lower revenue from admissions, dented by promotional activity. Adjusted EBITDA for the division sank 17%. The weakness in theme parks comes despite continued investment in the sector with the opening of a new coaster at Universal Studios Hollywood this quarter and Universal's largest theme park property, Epic Universe, last year. Theme park rival Disney reported record quarterly revenue in its park division in August. Cavanagh said on the earnings call that in addition to macroeconomic factors, Universal's theme parks struggled due to superior marketing from competitors and technological challenges at Epic Universe. Cavanagh cited new hires, including that of Luc Bondar to the role of chief brand and commercial officer for Universal Destinations and Experiences, as steps the company was taking to address these challenges. "Looking ahead, we expect performance to strengthen as we move through 2027, with a return to growth in the second half of the year," Cavanagh said. "We remain confident in the underlying strength of the business." Comcast's studios division reported revenue of $2.97 billion, down 1.1% from the third quarter last year. Adjusted EBITDA for the segment, however, increased 18.6% to $402 million, thanks to lower operating expenses. The July theatrical release of "The Odyssey," which became Universal's highest-grossing film of all time, boosted the division. Meanwhile, content licensing revenue was down 23.7% from the comparable quarter, leading to the decrease in studio revenue, according to Comcast. headlines.article_text: Procter & Gamble (PG) Q1 2027 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Procter & Gamble topped Wall Street's estimates for its quarterly earnings and revenue. The company updated its full-year sales forecast to reflect its acquisition of Thorne. CFO Andre Schulten said the company continues to see a bifurcated economy. In this article PG Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 7:50 07:50 P&G CFO Andre Schulten on Q1 results: Driven by 4% organic sales growth Squawk Box Procter & Gamble on Thursday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations, fueled by growing demand for its laundry detergent and home care products. Shares of the company rose more than 5% in morning trading. Here's what the company reported for the three-month period ended Sept. 30 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $2.00 adjusted vs. $1.88 expected Revenue: $23.3 billion vs. $22.8 billion expected P&G reported fiscal first-quarter net income attributable to the company of $4.73 billion, or $1.97 per share, down from $4.75 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year earlier. Excluding restructuring costs and other items, the company earned $2 per share. Net sales rose 4% to $23.3 billion. Bottles of Dawn dish spray are displayed for sale at a Target store on August 4, 2026 in Washington, DC. Kevin Carter | Getty Images P&G reported volume growth of 2.4%, a strong start for its new fiscal year. Like many consumer companies, P&G has seen demand for its products weaken as shoppers have become more value-conscious. Executives have previously said that consumers are now using every last drop of shampoo or laundry detergent, and value packs have become more popular. In fiscal 2026, P&G reported just one quarter of volume growth. P&G is still seeing signs of a bifurcated economy, CFO Andre Schulten said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Thursday. High-income consumers are willing to trade up to new products, even a $30 shampoo, while low-income consumers are trying to make brands like Tide and Pampers work for their tight budgets. The company has tried to address both ends of the spectrum with promotional pricing, new pack sizes and product innovation that can command higher prices. New premium products like Pampers Amore and Pantene's Abundant & Strong haircare line have helped P&G grow market share in those categories, executives said. Adding to P&G's challenges, the competitive environment is "intense," Schulten said on the company's quarterly earnings call. "We are getting the balance between pricing and product improvements, package improvements, claims, communication and retail execution right," Schulten told analysts. "But it's also a very fragile balance that we want to make sure we we don't compromise on, so we will price, and we will price with innovation, not jeopardizing the top-line momentum." P&G's top-performing division was fabric and home care, which includes brands like Tide and Febreze. The segment's volume rose 4.3% in the quarter, helped by stronger demand for laundry detergent and fabric enhancers. The company's baby, feminine and family care segment and its beauty business both reported volume growth of more than 2%. P&G's grooming division saw volume shrink 0.4% in the quarter. The segment includes Gillette and Venus razors. The company's healthcare business was the laggard of the portfolio this quarter. Its volume fell 2.9% as demand for oral healthcare products, like Crest toothpaste, and personal healthcare items, like Pepto-Bismol, shrank. The company is expecting continued "geopolitical and economic challenges," but P&G is on track to meet its guidance, CEO Shailesh Jejurikar said in a statement. For fiscal 2027, P&G reiterated its forecast for core earnings per share in a range of $6.89 to $7.11. The company is now projecting all-in sales growth in the range of 2% to 4% compared with the prior year, up from its previous outlook of 1% to 3%. The change reflects its acquisition of supplements brand Thorne , which closed Oct. 1. headlines.title: Blackstone's Jon Gray says CoreWeave can 'find a way through' financing pressure
headlines.summary: Blackstone COO Jon Gray says CoreWeave's underlying business is strong despite concerns over its mounting debt.
headlines.article_text: Blackstone's Jon Gray on CoreWeave financing pressure Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CoreWeave is facing challenges over the financing for their AI buildouts, but has a strong CEO, said Blackstone's Jon Gray. The company will "find a way through it," he said. Gray also said Blackstone delivered for its clients in the third quarter, and expects a robust fourth quarter ahead. In this article BX CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT VIDEO 8:23 08:23 Watch CNBC's full interview with Blackstone President and COO Jon Gray CoreWeave has been battered over concerns about its massive debt, but Blackstone chief operating officer Jon Gray believes the so-called neocloud company will weather the storm. Right now, CoreWeave and its neocloud peers are facing challenges over the capital needed to deliver on their promises, he said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk Box " Thursday. "Some of these companies have very talented CEOs. CoreWeave is a good example of this," Gray said. "They'll find a way through it, but that's the challenge they face. The underlying business is actually quite strong." CoreWeave has seen its stock sink , bond yields rise and spreads on its credit default swaps widen over the past week as investors became nervous about how the company will continue to finance its data centers, and at what cost. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Coreweave's one-month performance Demand for computing power, however, is strong, said Gray. He is seeing that across the board in the private companies the firm holds. At the same time, there is a constraint in delivering supply, he said. "For the neo clouds, if they can get to the other side, the pricing of compute is up 50%," he said. "Their legacy chips are worth much more than people thought. Their data centers are leased below market." Shares of CoreWeave sank 3.55% on Thursday, and are down 14% over the past week. Blackstone earnings Gray spoke with CNBC after Blackstone reported its third-quarter results, which came in mixed. Its stock was up 4% on Thursday. Blackstone saw quarterly revenue of $3.22 billion, short of the $3.28 billion expected from analysts polled by LSEG. Its adjusted earnings of $1.32 per share, however, topped the $1.26 consensus estimate. It was a "challenging quarter with markets" thanks to high energy prices and the rise in Treasury yields, Gray said. However, the firm delivered for its clients, he noted. "Across the board, our flagship strategies beat comparable public market indices and that's what we care most about," he said. Blackstone year to date He anticipates a strong fourth quarter and 2027, despite some cross-currents like the rising cost of capital, government deficits and some crowding out of capital due to the AI infrastructure build. However, good news is there is underlying economic and earnings strength, he said. Gray also expects initial public offerings to resume once the market and geopolitical situation calms a bit. He said investors just need to have some patience. "We have a long-term approach, and we feel very good about where we position capital for our investors, the growth of those companies, the growth of those assets, and that's what gives us confidence," he said. "At some point, the wider window will open, and when that happens, we and others will sell even more."
